title: The Mystery of the Missing Yeast Charm
markdown:
Moonlight spilled through the bakery windows and laid pale silver stripes across the flour-dusted floor. It was Lila’s favourite hour, when the street hushed and the ovens remembered they were allowed to be slow. Dough turned under her palms with a soft, living warmth. She kneaded with the patience of falling snow, apron dusted white, eyes holding a distant twinkle. Beside the hearth lay Bracken, a toast dragon, scales a warm brown like the skin of well-made sourdough. When he sighed, a puff of toasty air drifted out, smelling of hearth and home, and the little bells on the shop door did not even think of ringing.

“Almost time for the yeast charm, Bracken,” Lila murmured.

The charm was a tiny shimmer, a dewdrop of sleepy rise, kept in a velvet pouch among silken threads. It was what made her loaves tall and cloud-soft for the Harvest Feast.

She reached for the pouch. It was empty.

Her fingers paused on velvet. Bracken rumbled and nudged her hand with a velvety snout.

On the floor: little dark smudges. Scorched flour, delicate as whispers, leading toward a heavy wooden gateway in the far wall — the door to the old time room, where forgotten clocks kept their patient ticking.

“The time room,” Lila breathed.

Bracken nosed the gateway. It creaked like an old tree settling. Cooler air came out, damp stone and the perfume of years. The scorched marks wound down a narrow stair.

They followed, Lila with a small lantern, Bracken placing toast-warm paws as if the stone might bruise. Each step took them deeper. The ticking grew louder, a heartbeat in the dim, overlapping until it sounded like rain heard through wool. Tomorrow was the feast. Without the charm the loaves would sit down sadly in their tins, all crust and no cloud. Lila did not run. She went on, lantern-light sliding over gears that had forgotten whose hours they were for.

At the bottom the marks led to a dusty alcove. There, among worn woolen rags that held the warmth of many seasons, the yeast charm shone and threw tiny rainbows on the stone. Beside it slept a field mouse, whiskers twitching, a single sunflower seed clutched in paws no bigger than a teardrop.

Lila did not reach at once. She sat on her heels and let the clocks speak. Tick, and a pause. Tick, and another. Bracken’s sides rose and fell. Dust hung in the lantern beam like slow flour. The mouse’s seed gleamed like a small moon. For a long moment there was only that: stone cool under her knees, warm scales at her side, a creature dreaming of a feast the size of a crumb. The worry in her belly uncurled, then lay down, as if it too had found a rag to nest in.

Then the mouse stirred. Dark eyes opened. It saw Lila, saw Bracken, and shrank.

“Oh, little one,” Lila whispered. “Did you take the charm? Were you hoping to bake something of your own?”

The mouse gave a squeak like a sigh and nudged the charm forward with its nose. Lila understood. It had not meant harm. It had seen a shimmer and thought of growing, or of luck, or of a table no bigger than a thimble.

Bracken lowered his head and rumbled, then nudged the sunflower seed closer, as if to say the seed was already a treasure.

“This charm helps our bread rise,” Lila said. “Your seed looks a very fine one. Come tomorrow, if you like, and bring your friends. There will be crumbs enough, and a warm corner of crust.”

The mouse’s nose twitched in what might have been a nod. Lila lifted the charm. Its faint warmth settled into her palm like a known recipe. They climbed. The clocks soothed them all the way up.

Back in the bakery the moonlight had gone gentler, blue and silver. Lila returned the charm to its pouch. Bracken curled by the hearth and sighed a smell of bread and endings. Lila hummed a lullaby while she tidied, slow as the settling of fine flour. The little worry that had unfurled on the stairs folded itself away.

Outside, stars lay like tiny diamonds on dark velvet. The bakery was the coziest room in the sleeping street. Lila smiled a slow, sleepy smile. Tomorrow there would be a feast, and a mouse at the edge of it, and loaves that knew how to rise. Tonight all was well. Soon she and Bracken drifted toward star-dusted slumber, the yeast charm pulsing once, softly, like a heart that had found its pouch again.
characters: Lila (the midnight baker), Bracken (a toast dragon)
author: StoryGen Community
